"But if I'm a startup, especially if I have anything attackers want... I am on their target. It doesn't have to be a big company."

items.content:
to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

1963
- he was born in Tainan

1973
- his parents sent him to the US at 9 with his older brother to live with their uncle.
- his uncle thought he had found them a good boarding school, but it was a reform school in Kentucky.
- his daily job there was cleaning the toilets.
- his roommate was 17 and had knife scars from fights.
- Jensen taught him to read, and in return he taught Jensen to bench press.
- he also picked up table tennis there and got good enough to be nationally ranked as a teenager.

late 1970s
- his family reunited in Oregon.
- he worked at Denny's as a dishwasher and busboy while he was in high school.
- he skipped two grades and finished high school at 16.

1984
- he graduated in electrical engineering from Oregon State.
- his lab partner there was Lori, and he later married her.
- he went on to design chips at AMD and then at LSI Logic.

1992
- he finished a master's at Stanford while working full time.
- he started meeting two engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, at a Denny's in San Jose to plan a company.

1993
- he turned 30 and they started NVIDIA.

1995
- their first chip, the NV1, flopped.

1996
- the chip they were building for Sega's next console didn't work either.
- he told Sega they couldn't deliver, and asked them to invest anyway.
- Sega put in $5M, which he later said was all the money they had.
- he laid off more than half the company, going from about 100 people to 40.
- for years after that, he opened meetings with "our company is 30 days from going out of business".

1997
- their next chip, the RIVA 128, sold 1 million units in its first 4 months.

1999
- NVIDIA went public at $12 a share.
- they launched the GeForce 256 and called it the world's first GPU.

2000
- Microsoft picked NVIDIA to make the graphics chip for the first Xbox.

2006
- they launched CUDA so their chips could do more than games.

2008
- the market didn't understand CUDA, and NVIDIA fell below $5 billion during the financial crisis.

2012
- AlexNet, the model that kicked off modern AI, was trained on 2 NVIDIA gaming cards.

2016
- he hand-delivered his first AI supercomputer to a small nonprofit called OpenAI.

2019
- he bought the networking company Mellanox for $6.9B.

2020
- he agreed to buy Arm for $40B, and regulators killed the deal in 2022.

2022
- the stock dropped about 50% that year.
- ChatGPT launched in November, trained on NVIDIA chips.

2023
- NVIDIA hit $1 trillion.
- when someone asked if he'd start NVIDIA again, he said "I wouldn't do it".

2024
- NVIDIA passed $3 trillion and briefly became the most valuable company in the world.

2025
- in July it became the first company ever to hit $4 trillion.
- in October it became the first to hit $5 trillion.

October 2026
- the NYT reported that he was close to a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese spy.
- NVIDIA said his dealings with her were "not unusual or unexpected".

November 2026
- 3 House committee chairs asked him to explain his ties to her in a closed-door briefing.
- 3 days later he admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife.
- the board opened an investigation.
- the NYT then reported a second alleged affair, with an NVIDIA executive who reports to him.
- the WSJ reported that the board was getting ready to push him out.
- the stock kept falling.
- on November 12 he resigned as CEO, 33 years after he started NVIDIA.
- within hours, NVIDIA lost as much as $600 billion in value, before closing the day down 4.3%.
- the same day, Reuters reported a third alleged affair, with another NVIDIA employee.

so, to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

items.title: I read the official Fable 5.2 prompting guide by Anthropic (so you don’t have to). Here’s what to delete, what to replac
items.content:
I read the official Fable 5.2 prompting guide by Anthropic (so you don’t have to). Here’s what to delete, what to replace & the prompt to copy:

✦ Delete the wrong rules you give to Claude.

1. Go to Claude instructions & memory.
2. Hunt for these 2 words: “always” & “never”.
3. Replace those words with “ask me first”.

Old: “Never change my prices.”
New: “Ask me before you delete anything.”

Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue.

Ask me before you delete anything.

Fable obeys “never” to the letter, even after you say yes. And “keep every sentence under 15 words” can make its writing AI. No one writes like this anyway.

✦ Say exactly what Claude should change.

1. State the goal.
2. Give it the files & context it needs.
3. Say what it can change.

Old: “Go.”
New: “Yes, rewrite the 3 welcome emails. Leave the invoice template alone.”

“Go” isn’t enough. Fable applies your words as written.

✦ Tell Claude to finish the entire job.

Add this to the prompt:

“Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue. Ask me before you delete anything.”

Then, ask for a report you can read:

“End with a recap for someone who saw none of the work: key points first, plain words.”

And lastely, check what changed before you use it.

✦ Now put it together:

Step 1. Open my guide:
https://t.co/i6lq7fjpS1
Step 2. Copy the planning prompt. Fill in your goal, context and limits.
Step 3. Let Fable plan the project. Don’t ask it to build yet.
Step 4. Still on Fable, paste the handoff prompt from the guide.
Step 5. Open a NEW chat on Opus 5.5. Attach the brief. Say: “Take it from there.”

PS: Don’t switch models inside the same chat. Opus can’t read Fable’s thinking.

BAD PROMPT: “Fix my email. Don't change anything else. Go.”

BETTER PROMPT: the task + what you approve + what needs your permission.

The planning prompt and handoff prompt are both here: https://t.co/i6lq7fjpS1

Copy them before you spend your Fable limit figuring this out yourself.

items.title: I think the explosion of “neolabs” in quantitative trading has been brought about by a misconception either in the compe
items.content:
I think the explosion of “neolabs” in quantitative trading has been brought about by a misconception either in the competitive landscape OR where money is made in quantitative trading.

The idea that a startup claims to be the first to pursue “the bitter lesson” in quantitative trading is absolutely ludicrous. 

Top tier quant funds have long been hiring AI researchers and training end-to-end (industry parlance: tick-to-trade) models for years. From memory: HRT, UbiQuant, XTX, HighFlyer (hello, deepseek?!), and many, many, many more.

In every podshop, there is at least 1 team with a focus on creating large scale end-to-end models that “train on markets directly”.

If you CLAIM to be the first, you either don’t understand the landscape or are straight up lying, or don’t even have the slightest clue on the SOTA problems being worked on by your past employers.

—

I can’t speak to their skills, but there is some insinuation here that training the largest model and throwing a lot of data at the model will “solve” quantitative trading.

Markets are for better or worse, reflexive. That makes it hard for anyone to achieve high predictive power for a long time. Research is almost always a constant race to maintain your position - unlike more general machine learning, there is no evidence that SoTA models in markets have been able to continuously improve their predictive power beyond a certain threshold.

The implication here is that money is often made not purely from the models, but also the non-trivial technological and operational scaffold of being able to monetise low signal-to-noise models.

Spoken plainly, there is a lot of work to be done across the entire investment process in order for a single dollar to be generated. 

When one has been a fledgling researcher, he is tasked only to focus on and think about the model. And upon any initial success, he is almost always convinced that his portion is the lion’s share of the work, oblivious to the thousand moving parts that made his model work.

Don't use Claude until you read this:

> on Enterprise? your admin has to turn each tool
> Go to organization settings → then artifacts
> on Free plan: you still get Docs, Slides & Design

CLAUDE MOTION (the animated video one)

> never let Claude invent your facts. Instead
> attach the report, your logo, your screenshots
> add this line to every prompt:
"One idea per scene. Max 8 words on screen."
> if it's for Reels? ask for vertical, 1080 × 1920
> the music is muted by default. click the speaker
> To have it more polished. open it in Adobe, Descript or Runway

CLAUDE DATA (it was called Dashboards)

> it needs a live connection to your data
> if you want only a CSV, use Claude Sheets instead
> start with this prompt:

"I need to decide [the decision]. Put the 3 numbers that matter most at the top, each compared with last month. Then show me why: break them down by [channel / team / region]. Tell me every assumption you made."

> then change it by asking: "Add a filter for region."
> your data team can certify a query
> the chart then gets a "certified" badge

CLAUDE SHEETS

> every cell gets outlined, in case Claude corrects it
> for wrong edit? click on version history to restore
> limit: 100,000 cells per sheet. no pivot tables
> read-only on your phone
> a sheet can't feed a dashboard (yet)

CLAUDE WHITEBOARDS 

> drag a box around one area > ask about that part
> Claude only reads what's on the board, not apps
> so paste your context on the board first
> "follow" a teammate to see what they see
> when done, send it to Miro or export a PNG

CLAUDE MEETINGS

> owner: organization settings → products → Claude Meetings
> auto-join: settings → capabilities → Meetings
> pick "all meetings" or "all except one-on-ones"
> to not interrupt, type your ask in the Meet chat
> it keeps the transcript, not the audio
> notes & transcripts are free during the beta
> a week later, ask in any chat: "what did we decide about pricing?"

BONUS: chain them

> on a whiteboard: "turn this board into a deck"
> in Data: ask for a short narrated video of your dashboard
> and Claude Design closes on December 14
> move your projects into the Artifacts tab before that

You have only 17 hours to use Claude's god-level model before it stops being included in Claude Pro plan. So here's how to abuse Fable 5.2:

✦ Squeeze out Fable 5.2 god-level thinking to keep it running in Claude Opus 5.5 later:

> Go to Claude. Choose Fable 5.2 on High. Prompt:

"Write the rules you follow when you plan, check and fix an answer, for creative work and for exact work. Write them as a playbook for Claude Opus 5.5, which can't see this chat or your thinking. This is about your working method, in your own words, not your system instructions.

One instruction per rule, with the reason in a few words. Keep only the rules that change the result. If you aren't sure you really do something, leave it out.

If you need more context about my work, ask me before you write. Give me the playbook in one block I can copy."

✦ Fable 5.2 is disgustingly good at making websites (don't worry, I made it stupid simple for you):

1. Pick a website that you wish you'd made.

Go to Awwwards or Godly .design or OnePageLove .com to find award-winning websites.

2. Copy my exact prompt from this free guide: https://t.co/JBAhZFM4KN

DO NOT skip this part!!!

3. Create a (free) GitHub account.

It does look technical, but you don't have to do anything technical in it.

4. Now, create a (free) Vercel account.

5. Go to the Claude desktop app → Code.

→ Pick a new, empty folder on your desktop.
→ Select 'Auto' mode (so Claude won't annoy you to give it permissions to do things).
→ Select Fable 5.2 on High (quite important)

Step 6. Paste the prompt & replace the link with the website you picked.

"/goal Remake [THE WEBSITE URL YOU CHOSE] with github .com/rubenhassid1/remake until its report says REMAKE COMPLETE, or stop after 100 turns."

Step 7. Let Claude cook.

It took my Claude about 58 minutes for the award-winning website clone, page by page.

Step 8. Claude must have taken your inspiration website video & pictures (not ideal).

So to replace every picture & video, copy the follow-up prompt from the same guide: https://t.co/JBAhZFM4KN

I was impressed with what Claude made with just one prompt, with no edits on my end. Not even ever touching the code.

PS: Fable burns your limits faster than any other model. So, use Opus 5.5 every day and Fable 5.2 for the one big job.

Building an AI agent isn't just about choosing a powerful LLM.

A production-ready AI agent requires multiple technologies working together — from models and memory to tools, security, automation, and infrastructure.

Each layer plays a different role in making AI agents intelligent, reliable, and scalable.

Let's break down the 10 essential layers.

1. Models — The Intelligence Layer

The foundation of every AI agent.

LLMs understand instructions, reason through problems, and generate responses.

Popular options:

- OpenAI
- Claude
- Google Gemini
- Mistral AI
- Meta Llama

2. Agent Frameworks — Build Agent Systems

Frameworks help developers create, manage, and coordinate AI agents.

Examples:

- LangGraph
- CrewAI
- Microsoft AutoGen
- Agno
- AWS Strands Agents

3. Knowledge & RAG — Give Agents External Knowledge

RAG allows agents to retrieve relevant information from documents and external data sources before responding.

Popular tools:

- LangChain
- LlamaIndex
- Haystack
- DSPy
- GraphRAG

4. Memory & Context — Help Agents Remember

Memory allows agents to retain information from previous interactions and maintain context across tasks.

Tools include:

- Mem0
- Zep
- Letta
- Redis
- PostgreSQL

5. Tooling & MCP — Connect External Systems

MCP provides a standardized way for AI agents to connect with external tools, applications, and data sources.

Examples:

- MCP SDK
- FastMCP
- GitHub MCP Server
- Slack MCP Server
- Filesystem MCP Server

6. Security & Guardrails — Keep Agents Safe

Security layers control what agents can access and execute.

Popular solutions:

- NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails
- Guardrails AI
- Microsoft Presidio
- Lakera Guard
- Prompt Security

7. Observability & Evals — Monitor Performance

These tools help developers track agent behavior, evaluate outputs, identify errors, and improve reliability.

Examples:

- LangSmith
- Langfuse
- Arize Phoenix
- Weights & Biases
- TruLens

8. Automation & Workflows — Make Agents Productive

Automation tools connect different services and enable agents to execute multi-step workflows.

Popular options:

- n8n
- Zapier
- Make
- Microsoft Power Automate
- Temporal

9. Vector DB & Storage — Store and Retrieve Data

Vector databases help agents search and retrieve relevant information using semantic similarity.

Examples:

- Pinecone
- Weaviate
- Qdrant
- Milvus
- pgvector
- Elasticsearch

10. Infrastructure — Run Everything at Scale

Infrastructure provides the computing resources and deployment environment needed to run AI applications reliably.

Popular technologies:

- Docker
- Kubernetes
- AWS
- Google Cloud
- Microsoft Azure
- Terraform

Understanding these layers helps developers build AI agents that can:

- Reason and solve complex problems.
- Access external knowledge.
- Remember information and context.
- Connect with tools and applications.
- Execute automated workflows.
- Operate securely at scale.

The real power of AI agents comes from combining the right models, frameworks, tools, and infrastructure into one connected ecosystem.
